paragraphs: Vice President JD Vance said on X that the Iran war was why Republicans lost in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Al Jazeera. His post appeared to diverge from President Donald Trump's view. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote. He added: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so."

Trump acknowledged to Fox News that the attack on Iran and higher gasoline prices played a part, but said the move was justified. "People agree with what I'm doing on Iran, but they really probably weren't willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline," he said. He told The Wall Street Journal: "I did the right thing. I would have done it again."

Trump also pointed to other causes. In an interview with The New York Times he said, "I wasn't on the ticket," and that Republicans could not get enough people to vote as a result. He said some candidates he endorsed "fought me" and had flaws. On Truth Social he said Texas Gov. Greg Abbott would not have lost if he had not become a "RINO."

Republican strategist James Davis told Al Jazeera the war helped shift the electorate toward Democrats, but he said the biggest issue was a lack of a clearly articulated strategy. He said higher energy and diesel costs intensified concerns about affordability.

Trump said he does not plan any cabinet changes, calling the result "a point in time." He said he would work with Democrats but would be tough if they were not cooperative, and he posted a picture of a red cap reading "veto." Al Jazeera describes Vance as a likely 2028 presidential candidate.

Speaking at a Wednesday ceremony to raise the final steel beam of the White House ballroom, President Donald Trump said he "couldn't transfer the love" his supporters have for him to other Republican candidates, Fox News reported. It was his first public appearance since Democrats won the House and Senate. "If I were on the ballot, we would have won," he said. He spoke only about the ballroom until reporters asked questions.

Asked whether he agreed with Vice President JD Vance that the Iran war cost Republicans the election, Trump said, "I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term." He added that he would act the same way again: "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He said he had expected oil prices to rise much more when he decided to act.

Fox reported that Vance, in a long post, listed four steps for winning back voters: end the war, focus on cost of living and inflation, put America First, and change the relationship with Israel. Asked about it, Trump said, "I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine."
On Democrats, Trump said he would probably get along with them "unless they want to be destructive," and noted his veto power. He said Democrats had already called to talk.

Trump also told the Washington Examiner he is worried about impeachment "not even a little bit." He said it would "destroy the Democrat Party" and called it "impeachment for no reason." The pages did not report a Democratic response. The Examiner noted Democrats won sizable majorities in both chambers.
Trump was also asked about a Monday speech at the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. He said it "had nothing to do with anything else."

Republicans began assigning blame after Tuesday's midterm losses, with some directing criticism at President Donald Trump and others pointing to candidates or local factors. Democrats won in places such as Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, the BBC reported.

The BBC spoke to a dozen operatives, campaign officials and White House allies. Bill Miller, a Texas Republican lobbyist, said: "It's on him. It's not on anybody else." Gregg Peppin, a Minnesota Republican strategist, said the party saw "one mistake after another." A White House ally said disapproval of the Iran war, tariffs and the immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm."

Trump allies rejected that. They cited midterm history and said weak candidates hurt the party in Georgia, Michigan and Texas. One Texas operative, speaking anonymously, criticized Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. Krish Mathrani of the Michigan Republican Party called Trump "a turnout machine" and said his rallies raised enthusiasm.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis took a different approach at a Wednesday news conference, per Fox News. He called the results "close to an extinction level event for Republicans," noting that Florida would be the only one of the ten most populous states under Republican control. He credited a state ballot measure raising homestead property tax exemptions, which passed with about 62 percent, for drawing voters to the polls.

Pollster Doug Kaplan told Fox that DeSantis appears to be positioning himself for 2028 and called his remarks an "opening salvo" distancing himself from the party's Trump-led status quo. Strategist Mary Marslender said DeSantis was not distancing himself from Trump but taking credit for a winning record.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that he "wasn't on the Ballot" and would have won "IN A LANDSLIDE." The BBC said the result may force Republicans to consider their post-Trump future.

Democrats plan a broad set of investigations of the Trump administration now that they control Congress, NPR reported. With new majorities they will have full investigative powers, including subpoenas and compelled testimony. Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, said in a statement: "LAWYER UP."

Based on conversations with committee staffers, NPR said priorities include the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files and any connections to him. Democrats say many records were improperly redacted or withheld and that the Justice Department has tried to shield Trump. The department's leadership has denied that, and Trump has long denied wrongdoing and says his relationship with Epstein ended before 2016.

Other targets include the president's business interests, such as Truth Social and cryptocurrency projects, along with immigration enforcement, public health policy under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and executive power. Staffers said White House projects, including the East Wing remodel, a planned arch and the reflecting pool renovation, will face oversight.

Meanwhile, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Wednesday that no member of his caucus has talked to him about impeaching Trump, according to the Washington Examiner. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability because the House is a separate and co-equal branch of government," he said.

NPR noted that with Trump still in office, little major legislation is likely to become law, making oversight the main activity. Trump has said he can work with Democrats but has promised vetoes. The pages did not include a White House response to the investigation plans.

Inflation in the euro area rose to 4% in October, a three-year high, according to a flash estimate released Wednesday and reported by CNBC. The reading matched the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and was up from 3.8% in September.

Officials said the increase was largely due to energy costs. Energy inflation rose to 20.8% from 18.9% in September. CNBC notes that Europe is a net energy importer and is vulnerable to external energy shocks, and that prices have risen steadily since the start of the Iran war. October was the first time inflation has reached or topped 4% since September 2023, when it stood at 4.3%.

Rates varied across the 21 euro zone economies. Lithuania had the highest at 6.1% and Malta the lowest at 2.3%. Every country remained above the European Central Bank's 2% target. Policymakers said underlying inflation and wages were broadly stable despite the headline figure.

The ECB kept its key interest rate at 2.5% last month, after a 25 basis point hike in September. Shortly before the data came out, markets put the chance of a hike at the bank's final meeting of the year, in December, at 71.8%. After the release, that rose to more than 72%.

Robert Mertens, a senior analyst at Validus Risk Management, said ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy and on its capacity to bring inflation under control. He said that if French political unrest eased, the ECB could pursue a more aggressive path of rate rises, which he said would support the euro against the dollar.
On Wednesday morning the euro was up 0.6% against the dollar, and the yield on the 10-year German bund, a benchmark for euro zone bonds, was marginally higher.

Tariffs have emerged as a likely point of conflict between President Donald Trump and the incoming Democratic Congress, according to Foreign Policy and the BBC. Democrats won the midterm elections, and both outlets point to voter concern about prices as part of the backdrop.

Foreign Policy, in an analysis piece that is critical of Trump's trade policy, says exit polls showed the economy was voters' top concern and that about two-thirds of voters said the tariffs had hurt them economically. It cites a September poll in which 70 percent of Americans said the president should seek congressional approval before imposing new tariffs. It argues lawmakers now have a chance to reclaim trade authority, and that Trump has suggested he does not want to spend his last two years vetoing everything. Alan Wolff, a former Treasury official now at the Peterson Institute, said he knew of no sentiment in Congress on either side for the Section 338 tariffs used against Canada, which are being challenged in court.

The BBC is more cautious about what changes. It notes that Trump's tariffs were largely imposed by executive order, and that Trump told Fox News on Tuesday night he has the "ultimate power" of veto. Some Democrats have also backed certain tariffs to protect manufacturing jobs. The White House's response to the push in Congress was not reported in either article.

In Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford called the result "a victory for Canada." Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the results will not change anything in the short term and that Canada does not intend to speculate about what the new Congress might do. Prime Minister Mark Carney said US negotiators are "asking less and they're offering more." Former diplomat Colin Robertson said Canada has a window between now and January to finish a deal, though it remains to be seen how Trump will react.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race and will become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, NPR reported. Democrats also reclaimed control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Fox News.

El-Sayed, 42, is a former public health official. NPR says he campaigned on lowering costs, Medicare for All and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers was backed by President Trump and, according to NPR, repeatedly attacked El-Sayed over his Muslim faith and his opposition to U.S. military aid to Israel. Israel and the war in Gaza became a defining fault line in the race. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed beat in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers days before the election amid a bitter dispute over Israel.

Trump has announced plans to end roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year, without detailing how. The U.S. currently provides $3.8 billion a year under an agreement running through 2028. Speaking to NPR's Morning Edition, El-Sayed said the president is "actually right on this policy" and that he would also like to see the U.S. stop selling weapons to Israel, which he described using the words "genocide and apartheid." He also questioned U.S. military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Pakistan. Israel's response to these characterizations was not part of the reporting.
NPR says some Jewish and Black voters raised concerns about El-Sayed before the election. He said there is always more work to do but that the results challenged that narrative.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said El-Sayed's win "means so much to so many," citing the money spent against him and what Mamdani called racism and slander during the campaign.

Democrats will hold a majority of the nation's governorships after Tuesday's elections, Fox News reported. As of Wednesday morning, Democrats controlled 28 governorships and Republicans 20, with races in Kansas and Alaska not yet called.
That is a reversal from before the election, when Republicans held 26 governors' offices and Democrats 24. Democrats needed a net gain of at least two seats to claim the majority.

Fox notes that governors set state policy, approve or veto legislation, manage state agencies and direct responses to issues such as public safety, education, health care, immigration and abortion. They also oversee state elections and often become national party figures. The outlet says the new balance gives Democrats a broader bench of potential candidates ahead of the 2028 presidential contest.

The article says the shift could intensify disputes between Democratic governors and the Republican-led federal government over immigration enforcement, environmental rules, education policy and federal funding. It also says it could open the door to more lawsuits against the federal government, creating headaches for the Trump administration. The White House's response was not included.

Fox also stresses limits on the change. It does not automatically mean unified Democratic control of state governments, because Republicans still control many state legislatures. Legislative majorities, attorneys general and other elected officials will continue to shape how much power a governor has, and the impact will vary by state, especially where the governor's party does not control both chambers.
Looking ahead, Fox says Republicans will have fewer governorships to defend in the next cycle but will be working to prevent further losses in states where Democrats made gains.

Republican efforts to gain an advantage by redrawing congressional maps in the middle of the decade largely failed on Tuesday night, according to Fox News. The outlet reports that Democrats won battleground seats and some areas considered safe Republican territory in the midterms.

In Texas, where the Republican-led state government altered the map to favor the GOP in five districts, Democrats are projected to win at least three. Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar held their seats, and Democrats also won the newly redrawn 35th District. The other two had not been called.

In Florida, Republicans are on pace to lose all four seats they drew in their favor, Fox reports. Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz are projected winners in their altered districts, along with newcomer Pia Dandiya in a red-leaning seat. Rep. Darren Soto is narrowly ahead in a race too close to call. Fox notes Florida was still a bright spot for Republicans, as Byron Donalds won the governor's race and all Republican incumbents kept their seats.

In Ohio, a push to make districts held by Reps. Greg Landsman and Marcy Kaptur more favorable to Republicans also failed, and in Alabama Rep. Shomari Figures won another term despite his seat being altered to favor Republicans.

Two House Republicans, who were not named, told Fox the strategy was a mistake. One called it "definitely the wrong move" and said the party overreached. Another said Republicans in affected states had warned their governors for months.

Fox notes that redistricting is traditionally done after a census and that mid-decade changes drew bipartisan pushback, though both parties took part. In California, voters approved a referendum letting the legislature change its own map, which so far appears to have benefited Democrats.
Elon Musk spent heavily on Republican candidates in the midterms, and most of the races he backed were lost, according to Wired and the BBC.

Wired reports that by Wednesday morning candidates backed by Musk's America PAC had lost 20 races and won one, with 21 uncalled, based on its analysis of election data. It says Musk and his PAC have spent more than $400 million since Trump returned to office, and that of every traceable dollar he put into a race that has been decided, more than 99 cents went to a loser. America PAC did not respond to Wired's request for comment.

The most expensive contest was the Texas Senate race. Wired says a group funded with Musk's money routed through the Senate Leadership Fund spent $148 million through mid-October, and America PAC added $47 million. The BBC, citing the Financial Times, also reports the $47 million for Republican Ken Paxton and $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund in September. Democrat James Talarico won, and the BBC says the seat turned Democratic for the first time since 1988. Talarico said "all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas."
America PAC also ran ads in six other Senate races that have been called, and Wired says Musk's side lost all of them, including Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed won.

Musk posted on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time." The BBC reports Tesla and SpaceX shares were down 4.9% and 3.4% on Wednesday morning, while stocks were broadly up. Wired notes that Texas Democrats will oversee more than $1.6 billion in tax incentives that affect Musk's companies. Senator Ed Markey, a Democrat, wrote that Democrats would be "printing" many subpoenas, in response to a question on X.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, but the BBC reports they will face limits in turning that into law. Republican President Donald Trump keeps the power to reject legislation, and Congress can override a veto only with two-thirds majorities in both chambers, which Democrats alone will not have.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said, "Today begins the great American comeback." Senator Chris Coons told the BBC the party should not treat the result as a mandate, saying it remains "deeply unpopular" and must show it can deliver on wages and costs. He said the result was overwhelmingly a rejection of Trump, but warned that overreach or internal fighting could cause Democrats to miss the moment.

Democrats have more room on oversight. Rep. Robert Garcia, who will lead a powerful House oversight committee, said "Lawyer up" and listed possible targets including Trump's family, "corporate corruption," alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and ICE, and the handling of the Epstein files. The Senate can confirm or block cabinet and judicial nominees. The House can impeach, but conviction needs 67 Senate votes and is likely out of reach. The BBC says Democrats are debating impeachment, and Jeffries has said he has ruled nothing in or out.

Jeffries has said reversing Medicaid cuts and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits is a top priority. The BBC says bipartisan talks on issues such as affordability, AI regulation, Israel military funding and the Iran war could break down, and that Democrats may also split among themselves, particularly over Israel.
Trump told the New York Times, "We'll work with the Democrats." Minutes later he posted a picture of a red hat reading "VETO." The BBC says that mixed approach could become a theme.

Democratic wins in the U.S. midterms drew public reactions from governments and newspapers around the world, according to NPR and Fox News. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Trump congratulated them and said he was willing to work with them, while stressing that he would veto legislation he opposes, Fox reported.

In Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia is "sincerely" counting on Trump to continue his diplomatic efforts on Ukraine, and he pointed to trilateral talks planned for Abu Dhabi next week. Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov took a different tone, telling RIA-Novosti that the Democratic Party's activist wing takes an "extremely negative" approach to Russia.

European leaders were mixed. Spain's Pedro Sánchez wrote that Americans "voted against policies that only impoverish" and predicted a similar result in Spain's coming elections. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the world could now unite around the cost of living. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expects little to change, since Trump has mostly governed without Congress. His foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, hoped for more bipartisan discussion in Congress about supporting Ukraine. Norway's Jonas Gahr Stoere called the result a "powerful political signal."

Elsewhere, Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said Americans "said NO TO WAR." Japan's chief cabinet secretary said the alliance with the United States remains the cornerstone of Japan's policy regardless of the outcome. South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa said he expects a "new era in world relations," Reuters reported.

Trump said on Wednesday that the war in Iran, which has pushed up fuel prices, was part of the reason for the result. He also claimed Republicans would have won in a landslide had his name been on the ballot.

Ukraine says at least 40 people were killed when Russian glide bombs hit the southern village of Komyshuvakha, also spelled Kamyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday, according to the BBC and The Guardian. President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, and the search operation was in its third day.

Ukraine said nine glide bombs, some weighing 3,000 kilograms, struck as people gathered to receive humanitarian aid at a site near a local school. Zelensky said the first bombs hit people who came for aid, and then rescuers and police who arrived at the scene.

On Wednesday, Ukraine's national police released bodycam footage from a camera worn by one of the officers who was killed. It shows residents heading into an underground shelter, at least two floors deep, after the first strike. A voice on a two-way radio warns of more glide bombs, and an officer tells residents to go to the shelter. Seconds later the shelter is hit and the recording stops. The BBC said its verification team confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage of the aftermath released by Ukraine's state emergencies service.

Zelensky said there had been "very little reaction from the world" to what he called an "insane attack," and described it as one of "thousands" of Russian war crimes. The BBC reported that the Russian military had not publicly commented. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Russian and Ukrainian delegations are due to meet at the White House on Thursday at the invitation of first lady Melania Trump, according to the BBC. The meeting follows a six-day local ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region that allowed several hundred people to be evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. The ceasefire ended on Sunday.

The delegations include the two countries' human rights ombudsmen, Dmytro Lubinets and Yana Lantratova, who traveled together into Oleshky last week. Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, both veterans of peace negotiations, will also attend. Melania Trump is due to deliver remarks on the ceasefire on Thursday at 11:00 local time. The White House has shared no other details of the event.

The White House said she "independently initiated engagement" between the two sides and secured the ceasefire. The BBC reported that both Russia and Ukraine thanked her but did not describe her role. President Volodymyr Zelensky gave her the Order of Princess Olha, Ukraine's highest award for women, citing her "significant personal contribution" to humanitarian support.

The fighting continues. Al Jazeera reported that Ukrainian drone strikes killed three people in Russia's Belgorod region, according to local authorities. Zelensky said Russian attacks damaged power facilities in nine regions of Ukraine. Separately, Russian, Ukrainian and American representatives are due to meet in Abu Dhabi next week in the first trilateral talks since February, which US envoy Steve Witkoff said would focus on postwar security and de-escalation.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has begun consultations with political parties on who should try to form the next government, after receiving certified results from the 27 October election, the BBC reported. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, with 53 seats, nor opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc, with 48, reached a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Two Arab-led alliances won a record 19 seats combined.

Herzog told party leaders that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if they want to avoid a new election. Whoever he picks gets 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. All but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the vote not to work with the Arab-led parties.

The result has become a fight over legitimacy. Netanyahu's camp claimed Arab parties were "stealing" the election. Electoral officials said there was no evidence of irregularities, and committee chairman Noam Sohlberg warned that casting doubt on the results was "a real danger." He also said Shin Bet intelligence pointed to foreign money entering Israel and that more investigation was needed. Qatar's foreign ministry denied an allegation that it funded Arab turnout.

Al Jazeera reported that Palestinian citizens of Israel face police raids, arrests and interrogations since the vote. Joint List leaders said the claims are a smear, and Ahmad Tibi said there was no sign of manipulation in Arab towns. Itamar Ben-Gvir urged the arrest of Arab party leaders. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported Shin Bet request to question four Arab politicians for lack of evidence, and Likud accused her of obstructing the investigation. Herzog said Arab citizens "must not be smeared."

The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said on Wednesday that cold storage rooms holding its blood products were affected by the recent wave of cyberattacks on European refrigeration systems, according to the BBC and CNBC. Until now, only supermarkets were known to have been hit.

CNBC reported that the EFS was not the direct target. Cold storage units run by external providers were compromised at three of its sites on Monday, with temperature and defrost thresholds set "to excessively high levels." The units hold blood products before delivery to hospitals, along with samples for biobanks and frozen plasma. The EFS said its monitoring systems reacted quickly. Staff either brought the equipment under control or took it offline, and moved samples to other facilities. It said no health impact had been identified and no blood products were lost. It is working with France's national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry.

Nobody has been formally identified as responsible. The BBC reported that the Russian groups Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they hacked equipment maker Danfoss, which fueled speculation. French security firm Sekoia said it has no technical evidence of Russian-speaking groups and is skeptical of the claim, noting Noname057 is mainly known for denial-of-service attacks. Sekoia said Iranian-aligned actors are also possible, and experts did not rule out teenagers.

Researchers using decoy freezer systems saw scanning only in Europe, and one expert said the simultaneous timing points to planning and coordination. Authorities in several countries are investigating and warning supermarkets about future attacks.

Binance said on Tuesday that the hackers who targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from the exchange spent months preparing, according to Ars Technica. The FBI and the firm TRM Security attributed the heist to North Korean actors. Binance said it has frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of the total and has set aside funds to cover the loss.

The company described a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that began no later than June. In June, an engineer downloaded a tampered version of the Homebrew software tool. In September, another engineer was contacted through a job-hunting platform by someone posing as a project director. After two fake interviews, he was told to download an "assignment" that contained malicious code. Binance said the malware was not caught by its endpoint security tools.

On October 20, the attackers used that laptop and an internal AI tool to take control of two other engineers' devices. On the 29th, they used a stolen credential from one of them to deploy a container and start the transfers. They also reached an internal wallet signing service, which let them complete transactions outside the normal withdrawal process.

Binance said it received an alert about large transfers and began investigating immediately. It suspended withdrawals and worked with partners to freeze tokens. That did not stop everything, because the attackers had used an Ethereum mechanism called EIP-7702 to create on-chain authorizations that worked independently of Binance's systems. Because the hot wallet used multi-party computation, Binance had to develop a special procedure to revoke them, which took extra time.

The World Health Organization has approved clinical trials of two new vaccines designed for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, as the Democratic Republic of the Congo faces the largest outbreak in its history, Al Jazeera reported. WHO expert groups recommended adding the trials on Monday. Results are expected in early 2027, according to the WHO.

The outbreak was declared on 15 May. The Africa CDC says 10,444 cases have been confirmed, and Al Jazeera reported that more than 5,300 people have died. The virus has a 50 percent fatality rate and no treatment or vaccine designed for it. A trial that began last month uses Ervebo, a vaccine approved for a different strain. The new vaccines were developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India and Moderna, and the trial is led by the DRC's National Institute for Biomedical Research.

WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said vaccines are not substitutes for early care, contact tracing, isolation, safe burials and community engagement. He urged countries to lift travel restrictions, saying they discourage transparent reporting.

The disease has spread beyond the DRC. Kenya has reported nine cases, including two deaths, and Nigeria has confirmed one case, according to the WHO. The Guardian reported that it has also reached Uganda.

Meanwhile, a British healthcare worker sent to help with the response has tested positive and is being evacuated to the UK, a government spokesperson said. The patient is stable and expected to arrive by Thursday before moving to a high-consequence infectious disease unit. The government said the risk to the UK public remains low.

Google is facing criticism over a new policy for schools that affects how its AI features and Search are offered. After The New York Times reported that Google would turn off Search for schools that reject AI entirely, Sen. Bernie Sanders called the policy "extortion" and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google was trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into public schools, CNBC reported. Former FTC Chair Lina Khan said it showed the danger of letting an unregulated monopolist control an essential service.

Google responded on X that the policy gives schools more choice. It said Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default, and schools can enable them individually. It also said AI Mode and AI Overviews in Search for schools will walk students through problems step by step rather than give quick answers. Google did not directly address the claim that Search access requires accepting AI. Chris Phillips, a Google vice president for education, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated."

Wired reported that Google is declining to let schools switch off AI Overviews, so schools wanting to avoid them would have to block Search. Some educators and parent groups called the move frustrating. A former Google Search product manager said maintaining a separate version of Search would be hard, while another critic noted Microsoft offers an extension that turns off AI summaries in Bing. Los Angeles Unified said it is still reviewing the implications.
DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools as an alternative, and its CEO pointed to instructions for changing a school's default search engine, TechCrunch reported.

SpaceX has signed a multiyear deal with Qualcomm to provide key network technology for Starlink Mobile, its service positioned as a challenger to Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile, CNBC reported. Qualcomm said on Wednesday that the terrestrial network it will help build will "complement Starlink's satellite capabilities," with a rollout planned to begin next year. Financial terms were not disclosed.

SpaceX will use Qualcomm's Dragonwing cellular infrastructure hardware and software in base stations. A Qualcomm executive, Durga Malladi, said the companies are building cellular infrastructure in the United States, advancing 5G now with an opportunity to lay the foundation for 6G. SpaceX plans to use the technology to set up tens of thousands of new cell sites. It has not named partners among cell tower companies or said how many towers may be needed. Carriers generally lease space from firms such as American Tower and Crown Castle.

The deal fits a broader push. Starlink made up 36 percent of SpaceX's third-quarter revenue and 85 percent of its operating profit, but its satellite network cannot yet deliver all the voice, video and data coverage that rivals offer on smartphones. Last month SpaceX announced an agreement to buy a nationwide spectrum portfolio in the 800 MHz band, which sent shares of U.S. carriers lower. The Washington Post reported this week that SpaceX is in talks to acquire EchoStar's Boost Mobile.

Qualcomm is best known for chips inside devices rather than base stations, though it has pushed into 5G infrastructure since 2020 and has earlier deals with Verizon, Dish and Vodafone. SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for more information.

Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, according to the BBC. The government says the move will help Hungarian society heal from 45 years of communist rule. From Wednesday, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services are available on a website, nyitottaktak.hu.

The date is symbolic: on 4 November 1956, Soviet tanks entered Budapest and other cities to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution. Prime Minister Péter Magyar, speaking at the state archives in Budapest, asked everyone to treat the publication "with dignity and humanity". He warned that many families will face difficult information, often about a deceased relative. Opening the files was a central promise of his campaign before his April election victory, and he described it as fulfilling a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989.

The BBC says earlier governments of different political stripes considered opening the files but did not. Since 1998 people could apply for their own file and historians could research others, but many names were blacked out and many files were withheld by post-communist secret services. Many were also shredded around 1988-89. A typical entry lists the informer's real name, codename, date of birth, address, mother's name, motive for recruitment and handling officer. Intimate details used for blackmail will be edited out.

Critics say the move is too late, the files are incomplete, and it risks division and anguish for relatives. Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP for the far-right Our Homeland party, said that in most surviving agent reports the agent cannot be identified, let alone their motives, and that publishing names without context risks misleading the public. Historian Krisztian Ungváry, a long-time campaigner for access, said citizens have a right to know what the state recorded about them.

Another batch, the "B-dossiers", is being digitised and will be released on 25 February. These should give more detail on how people were recruited and how valuable their information was. An estimated 150,000 to 160,000 people were recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990.

Millions of dollars of food grown in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been shipped to Australia labelled "produce of Israel", according to analysis by the human rights legal organisation Global Echo, reported by The Guardian. The group examined commercial documents and official trade data from the Israeli government and the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Global Echo analysed 132 agricultural shipments from Israel to Australia between August 2018 and August 2026. It found 85 of them, or 64 percent, contained settlement products, with at least US$5 million of organic dates grown in settlements. Between January 2025 and August 2026, 20 of 24 date shipments analysed came from settlements, including places such as Netiv Hagdud, Beit Haarava and Naaran.

Israel's settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, the report says. Israeli law requires exports to be labelled as from Israel unless the destination country prohibits such labelling. Australia has no law banning settlement imports and no requirement to label their origin.

Global Echo's executive director, Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, said Australian consumers would likely find this startling and may be contributing to the occupation. She said European import bans could push exporters toward markets such as Australia. Human Rights Watch researcher Sarah Sanbar said trade is one of the lifelines of illegal settlements.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the Senate in September that the settlements were illegal but said Australia was not pursuing a blanket import ban, citing concerns about unintended consequences for Australian businesses. Countries including the UK, Spain, Belgium, Ireland and the Netherlands have announced or imposed bans. A foreign affairs department spokesperson said Australia is pursuing further targeted measures with international partners. The Israeli embassy in Canberra did not respond to a request for comment. Israel's ambassador, Hillel Newman, earlier told The Australian the settlements issue had been blown out of proportion and that following the UK's example would be a mistake.

FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is going through "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel. De Miguel, 30, a father of one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, died after a serious injury in a collision with Owono in a Spanish second division match on Monday.

The collision happened seven minutes into stoppage time with the score 2-2. Owono ran toward the centre circle to clear a long ball and his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel, who lay motionless and was taken to hospital by ambulance. Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.

In a statement released by his club on Wednesday, the 25-year-old said he struggled to find words and felt enormous pain over the loss. He said he knew there would be many issues to address and would face them with the utmost respect. Team-mate Lautaro Spatz said Owono would never intentionally hurt anyone and was deeply affected. Owono did not attend a voluntary training session, and has deactivated his Instagram account. Equatorial Guinea's football federation president, Venancio Tomas Micha, offered Owono "all our human and professional backing".
Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter. Under Spanish law, any death deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.

Tenerife began six days of mourning, suspending club activities. The funeral will be in Navahermosa, Toledo, attended by the club's players, staff and officials. Tenerife will open its stadium on Saturday evening for supporters to say farewell. The weekend matches against Granada and Mallorca, involving Tenerife and Andorra respectively, were postponed. Minutes of silence were held at European matches this week, and Spain's football federation postponed Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina games.

Sequoia Capital published a memo on X on Wednesday titled "The Sequoia of Tomorrow," saying it has raised roughly $10 billion in new funds. According to TechCrunch, the firm is also closing its London office, shutting its Arc accelerator and its Scouts program, merging its early-stage and growth teams, flattening its partnership and ending the Monday partner meeting.

TechCrunch describes the changes as a return to an earlier, smaller firm focused more narrowly on Silicon Valley. Sequoia itself describes coming out of a roughly 20-year expansionary phase that, it says, had the unintended side effect of hierarchy. Scouts, launched around 2009, gave small checks to founders and operators to invest on the firm's behalf. Arc, launched in March 2022, was a batch accelerator for pre-seed and seed founders, with admitted companies getting $500,000 to $1 million up front.

On London, the memo says, "We simply don't see the need for a local presence," adding that Europe will keep producing "outlier founders" that Sequoia can support from the Bay Area. Luciana Lixandru, hired in 2020 as the firm's first partner in Europe, wrote on X that she was offered a move to San Francisco and declined. She says she remains a partner, will keep her board seats and will invest personally in European founders. TechCrunch notes that Andreessen Horowitz and Coatue also closed London offices.

The memo says seven general partners now primarily own and operate the firm: co-stewards Alfred Lin and Pat Grady, along with Andrew Reed, Shaun Maguire, Konstantine Buhler, Sonya Huang and David Cahn. Stephanie Zhan has left to launch her own firm, and Jess Lee is now listed as chief product officer. The memo acknowledges the moves carry costs: "It is scary to break something that's already working just fine."

Investors in Revolut have completed a secondary share sale that values the British fintech at $115 billion, according to TechCrunch. That is 53% more than the valuation set in a share sale a year earlier. The sale brought no new money into the company, and Revolut declined to say how much stock was sold. It was led by investors including Glade Brook Capital Partners, Coatue, Durable Capital Partners, T. Rowe Price Associates and Baillie Gifford.

Founded in 2015 by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko, Revolut now has more than 80 million retail customers in over 40 countries. This year it launched banks in the U.K., Mexico, Australia and New Zealand, and it has secured banking licenses in France, Colombia and Argentina. It has also begun rolling out services in India. TechCrunch reports the company had profit margins of 38% on revenue of $6 billion in 2025.

In the United States, Revolut has conditional approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to establish a national bank. It plans to launch in the first half of 2027, subject to final regulatory approval.

Business banking accounts for about 20% of gross profit, said James Gibson, head of Revolut Business. The company told TechCrunch the unit processes more than £36 billion in monthly transactions and holds more than £18 billion in deposits. Gibson said Revolut wants to expand business banking to Mexico, Brazil and India, without giving a timeline, and to grow from over 800,000 business customers to a million by 2027.
Storonsky has considered a dual listing in New York and London, with a preference for a primary U.S. listing. TechCrunch says an IPO would come no earlier than 2028, depending on market conditions.

The U.S. Air Force wants to develop mobile 3D concrete printers that can erect buildings quickly, as many U.S. bases in the Middle East have been damaged by Iranian bombardment, according to Defense News. The service laid out its aims in a Small Business Innovation Research solicitation that closes in January 2027.

The solicitation says the Air Force has spent decades building advanced targeting and strike capabilities while often housing the airmen who sustain them in tents, trailers and flat-walled structures "never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead." A September 2026 report by the Defense Department Office of the Inspector General found that hundreds of U.S. military buildings across eight Middle Eastern countries were damaged by Iranian attacks.

Concrete printing, in which machines deposit layers of material to form structures, is gaining ground in commercial construction. The Air Force used 3D printing to rebuild hurricane-damaged Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida in 2023, and a Maryland Air National Guard civil engineer squadron is developing its own mobile printer. But the Air Force says current technology has not yet solved the combined problem of printable expeditionary materials, workflows usable in the field, and shapes designed to limit blast and fragmentation effects.

The project, which goes straight to Phase II, will test cement-like materials for strength, adhesion and local availability. It will also develop geometries meant to reduce blast reflection and interrupt fragmentation paths. The Air Force wants a printer that lightly trained personnel can operate in austere conditions. It sees dual-use applications such as critical infrastructure and humanitarian relief, though it notes that commercialization will likely require approvals under building codes.

As the Pentagon works to rebuild its munitions stockpile for the Iran war, it is relying partly on aging Army ammunition plants, several of which have long records of environmental and safety violations, according to reporting by The War Horse published by Defense News.

The report focuses on the Radford Army Ammunition Plant in Virginia. When Hurricane Helene flooded the New River in 2024, water washed more than a dozen storage containers of chemicals out of the plant, including dibutyl phthalate, a rocket propellant component linked to cancer and reproductive problems. The Army did not warn residents until weeks later. Two years on, three containers remain unaccounted for, according to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, which found more than 1,500 gallons leaked into the environment. Radford had been cited for excessive pollutant discharges in 2023 and 2024, and Virginia regulators listed it as the state's top releaser of toxins in 2022.

Radford is the only domestic producer of certain propellants for artillery and rockets. Alyssa Carpenter of Citizens for Arsenal Accountability said, "You can't increase production without increasing the toxic byproducts." Mathy Stanislaus, a former Environmental Protection Agency official, said the Defense Department's record is "not good." The Army's response was not included in the supplied text.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that Patriot interceptor inventory fell from more than 2,300 at the war's start to around 800 by the end of July, and THAAD stocks fell by nearly half. The report says the strain predates the war, and that the Pentagon has recently put billions toward 155 mm artillery shell production.

South Africans voted in local elections on Wednesday, with the African National Congress expected to remain the largest party but to fall short of a third of the vote, according to The Guardian. Polls showed the ANC below the 45.6% it won in 2021 municipal elections and the 40.2% in the 2024 national elections. Voters cited water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

Many of the country's 257 municipalities already run on unstable coalitions, which analysts cited by The Guardian blame for poor service delivery. Johannesburg has had 10 mayors in 10 years, Ekurhuleni has had three since 2021, and Tshwane's mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. Johannesburg is currently led by ANC mayor Dada Morero in coalition with the Economic Freedom Fighters and the Patriotic Alliance.

In Johannesburg, the Democratic Alliance's Helen Zille has run a high-profile campaign, though The Guardian reports she is viewed with suspicion by many black voters over past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba, polling around 10%, has ruled out working with her and has called her a racist, which she denies. In eThekwini, which includes Durban, Jacob Zuma's MK party was polling above 40%, while the ANC was at around 10%. The DA looks set to keep its Cape Town majority with less than its 58% from 2021.

The electoral commission has a week to announce final results, and parties then have two weeks to form councils and elect mayors. South African media report the ANC's national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, while local leaders reportedly are not.

The UK Supreme Court began hearing a challenge on Wednesday to last year's decision to proscribe Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation, a step that placed it alongside groups such as al-Qaida and Boko Haram. The challenge was brought by Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the group. The hearing is due to conclude on Thursday, with judgment expected at a later date, according to The Guardian.

Raza Husain KC, representing Ammori, told the five judges that Palestine Action never advocated violence against the person. He argued that suffragettes, anti-war, environmental and animal rights groups used similar or more extreme tactics without being proscribed. He said the ban had affected the wider Palestinian solidarity movement and chilled the expression of journalists, academics and artists. Ammori argues that proscription disproportionately interferes with freedom of speech and protest.

For the home secretary, Sir James Eadie KC said in written submissions that the Court of Appeal's decision was lawful and proportionate. He cited the convictions of four people, including one for grievous bodily harm, and a finding of a "terrorist connection" in the raid on an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, near Bristol. He also pointed to US sanctions on the group. Eadie said proscription does not prevent public expressions of support for the Palestinian cause or demonstrations targeted at Elbit.

At least 25 protesters were arrested outside the court, including Sir Jonathon Porritt, a former director of Friends of the Earth. They held placards adapting a tweet by Sarah Helm, which police had judged did not meet the criminal threshold for supporting a terrorist organisation.

Thousands of students marched in Copenhagen on Monday against a government plan to cut Denmark's student stipends, adding to a wave of youth protests across Europe, according to Al Jazeera. Organisers said up to 13,000 people marched from the city hall square to parliament under the banner "Enough is Enough" over cuts meant to free up money for defence spending. Student associations said some 40,000 students were on strike at 57 schools.

Since 1970, every Danish student over 18 has automatically received the allowance regardless of parental income. Students currently get 1,154 kroner a month if they live with their parents and 7,426 kroner if they live alone. Under the proposal, the allowance would be abolished for students living with parents earning over 700,000 kroner a year. Only those whose parents earn between 419,589 and 700,000 kroner would qualify, with payments staggered by income. The Higher Education Ministry said around 14,000 students are expected to lose their stipends and about 8,000 would see them reduced.
The government has also proposed that unemployment benefits for recent graduates go only to those who worked during 18 of the last 24 months of their studies.

Oscar Tonsberg Hoffmann, president of the Danish High School Students Association, told AFP that it would be wrong to dismantle "one of the world's strongest educational systems." Student Kieran Hindshaw said he felt betrayed by a government that includes left parties. Industry Minister Martin Lidegaard, who leads the Social Liberal Party, said the cuts "are not pleasant decisions." Al Jazeera links the protests to similar student demonstrations in France that spread to other countries and broadened into complaints over living costs and housing.
